items.stem: Read this from the opening of a story, ‘The Last Ferry’: ‘She reached the jetty in time to see its lights shrink across the black water’ Where is Mira when the story begins?
options: At the church on the hill
At the jetty, just after the ferry has left
On the ferry, crossing the water
items.answer: At the jetty, just after the ferry has left
items.markingKey: Retrieval: the answer is stated in the quotation (‘She reached the jetty in time to see its lights shrink across the black water’).

items.stem: In the opening of a story, ‘The Last Ferry’ the writer writes: ‘Her aunt had promised to meet her. Her aunt had promised a great many things.’ What does this suggest about Mira’s feelings towards her aunt?
items.answer: It suggests Mira does not fully trust her aunt. The repetition of ‘promised’ and the phrase ‘a great many things’ imply the aunt often breaks her word, so Mira is disappointed but not surprised.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: inference (distrust, disappointment, aunt is unreliable); supported by the repetition of ‘promised’ or ‘a great many things’; credit for noting the weary, unsurprised tone

items.stem: In the opening of a story, ‘The Last Ferry’ the writer writes: ‘for a long moment she simply stood there’ What does this suggest about how Mira reacts to missing the ferry?
items.answer: She is stunned and does not know what to do; ‘simply stood’ and ‘a long moment’ show she is frozen by shock or disappointment.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: shock/uncertainty/defeat; reference to ‘simply stood’ or ‘long moment’

items.stem: Read this sentence from the opening of a story, ‘Nobody Believes Me’: ‘which I have, for nearly a whole term’ What does this reveal about the narrator? Answer in your own words and support your answer with a short quotation.
items.answer: The narrator is over-confident and exaggerates their expertise; ‘nearly a whole term’ is a tiny amount of study, which makes their claim comic.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: point (inference) + evidence (short quotation) + explanation of how the words create that impression. 1 mark: over-confident/boastful/naive; 1 mark: explains the humour of ‘nearly a whole term’.

items.stem: Read this sentence from an extract from a story, ‘The New Captain’: ‘Rosa, who was now examining her boots with great concentration’ What does this suggest about Rosa’s feelings? Make an inference and support it with close reference to the words of the text.
items.answer: Rosa is embarrassed or jealous because she expected to be captain; she pretends to be busy to hide her disappointment.
items.markingKey: Award up to 5 marks from: point (inference) + evidence (short quotation) + explanation of how the words create that impression. 1 mark: disappointment/jealousy/embarrassment; 1 mark: explains the pretence in ‘with great concentration’.

items.stem: Read an extract from a story, ‘The Radio Mender’. ‘Dada Farouk’s stall was the smallest in the market, but people queued for it anyway. He sat on an upturned crate, sleeves rolled to the elbow, mending radios with fingers as quick and careful as a bird building a nest. He never hurried and never apologised for not hurrying. “A thing done fast is a thing done twice,” he told a customer who tapped his watch. When a boy came up clutching a cracked phone and a fistful of coins, Dada Farouk looked at the coins, then at the boy’s worn shoes, and pushed the money back across the counter. “Pay me when you are rich,” he said, already unscrewing the case. The boy opened his mouth to argue. Dada Farouk raised one grey eyebrow, and the boy closed it again.’ How does the writer present Dada Farouk as a character?
items.answer: Skilled (bird simile), patient and confident (never hurried), wise (proverb), generous and observant (worn shoes, pushes coins back), respected (queue, eyebrow). Methods: description, dialogue, action, reactions of others.
items.markingKey: Level-marked: top band (3–4) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (2) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1) mainly retelling. [4]

items.stem: In the opening of a story, ‘The Last Ferry’ the writer writes: ‘A single gull picked at a crust beside the bins, unbothered.’ Why might the writer include the detail of the gull?
items.answer: The gull is calm and ‘unbothered’, which contrasts with Mira’s difficult situation and emphasises how alone she is: nobody else in the scene cares.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: contrast with Mira’s distress or emphasis on emptiness; explanation using ‘single’ or ‘unbothered’

items.stem: A story told by a character using ‘I’ is written in which narrative perspective?
items.answer: first person
items.markingKey: First person: the narrator is a character in the story and uses ‘I’/‘me’.

items.stem: Explain how the choice of a third-person omniscient narrator shapes what the reader learns in this extract: ‘In the kitchen, Mrs Mensah was worrying about money; upstairs, her son was listening at the door, convinced she was angry with him; neither knew that the letter on the table would solve everything.’
items.answer: Third-person omniscient narrator: the narrator knows the thoughts of more than one character and even what will happen next.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying third-person omniscient narrator; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the narrator knows the thoughts of more than one character and even what will happen next.

items.stem: Explain how the choice of a third-person omniscient narrator shapes what the reader learns in this extract: ‘The villagers believed the well was cursed. The well, of course, knew nothing about it; it simply held its water in the dark, as it had for three hundred years.’
items.answer: Third-person omniscient narrator: an all-knowing narrator comments on the villagers’ beliefs from above and knows the well’s whole history.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying third-person omniscient narrator; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: an all-knowing narrator comments on the villagers’ beliefs from above and knows the well’s whole history.

items.stem: Rewrite this extract using a different narrative viewpoint, then explain one thing that changes for the reader: ‘I pressed my ear to the door. Whatever they were arguing about, it was about me.’
items.answer: Model rewrite: ‘Kofi pressed his ear to the door. Whatever they were arguing about, he was sure it was about him.’ The change of viewpoint alters how close the reader is to the character’s thoughts.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for consistent change of pronouns and verb forms; 1 for keeping the meaning; remaining mark(s) for explaining the effect (closeness, knowledge, reliability). Original: first-person narrator.

items.stem: What is an omniscient narrator?
options: A narrator who knows the thoughts and feelings of all the characters
A narrator who only knows one character’s thoughts
A narrator who is the main character
A narrator who speaks to the reader as ‘you’
items.answer: A narrator who knows the thoughts and feelings of all the characters
items.markingKey: Omniscient = all-knowing; often third person.

items.stem: What does ‘show, don’t tell’ mean a writer should do?
options: reveal character through actions, speech and detail rather than stating traits directly
tell the reader exactly what each character is like
items.answer: reveal character through actions, speech and detail rather than stating traits directly
items.markingKey: Showing lets the reader infer: ‘She slammed the door’ instead of ‘She was angry’.

items.stem: Read: ‘Whenever Aunt Bisi entered a room, conversations stopped and children remembered urgent business elsewhere.’ What does this suggest about the character? Explain how the writer shows this through how other characters react to them.
items.answer: How other characters react to them: others fear or respect her, so she is formidable.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying how other characters react to them; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: others fear or respect her, so she is formidable.

items.stem: Read: ‘Rosa, who was now examining her boots with great concentration’ What does this suggest about the character? Explain how the writer shows this through what the character does (action).
items.answer: What the character does (action): Rosa pretends to be busy, which reveals her hurt pride.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying what the character does (action); further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: Rosa pretends to be busy, which reveals her hurt pride.

items.stem: Read: ‘Ravi wondered, not for the first time, whether anyone would notice if he simply stopped talking altogether.’ Using point, evidence and explanation, analyse what this reveals about the character.
items.answer: The character seems lonely: his private thought reveals loneliness and a feeling of being ignored.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for a valid trait (lonely or similar); 1 for apt evidence; remaining mark(s) for explaining how the words create the impression (the character’s thoughts and feelings).

items.stem: Read: ‘She counted the money twice, then a third time, then hid it inside the hollow leg of her bed.’ Using point, evidence and explanation, analyse what this reveals about the character.
items.answer: The character seems cautious and secretive: repeated counting and hiding suggest she is cautious, anxious or secretive.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for a valid trait (cautious and secretive or similar); 1 for apt evidence; remaining mark(s) for explaining how the words create the impression (what the character does (action)).

items.stem: What is the main purpose of a story’s opening?

To explain how the story ends

items.stem: A story begins: ‘“Nobody leaves this room until I find out who did it,” said Mr Lim.’ Explain why this opening might make a reader want to continue.
items.answer: Opening with dialogue: the dramatic line establishes conflict, a mystery and a commanding character.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying opening with dialogue; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the dramatic line establishes conflict, a mystery and a commanding character.

items.stem: A story begins: ‘The ice cracked under Hana’s left boot, then under her right.’ Explain why this opening might make a reader want to continue.
items.answer: Starting in the middle of the action (in medias res): beginning at the moment of danger creates instant tension.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying starting in the middle of the action (in medias res); further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: beginning at the moment of danger creates instant tension.

items.stem: Read an extract from a story, ‘The New Captain’. ‘Coach Adeyemi blew the whistle so hard that a pigeon left the roof. “Captain,” she said, and pointed at Lena. A murmur ran round the changing room. Lena was not the fastest player, nor the loudest; that was Rosa, who was now examining her boots with great concentration. Lena stood up slowly. “Me?” “You,” said the coach. “You’re the only one who passes the ball when you could shoot.” Rosa snorted. Lena felt her face burn, but she crossed the room, sat down beside Rosa and said quietly, “I’ll need you up front on Saturday. Nobody scores like you.” Rosa looked up. For a second she said nothing. Then, very slightly, she nodded.’ How does the writer show the tension between Lena and Rosa, and how it is resolved? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Rosa’s pretended interest in her boots; the snort; Lena’s burning face; Lena’s quiet praise ‘Nobody scores like you’; the pause and slight nod.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12 (reading). Indicative content: Rosa’s pretended interest in her boots; the snort; Lena’s burning face; Lena’s quiet praise ‘Nobody scores like you’; the pause and slight nod.

items.stem: In the opening of a story, ‘Nobody Believes Me’ the writer writes: ‘Yes, I was in the garden. Yes, I had the cricket bat. And yes, the ball did happen to be lying among the broken glass’ How does this make the reader doubt the narrator?
items.answer: The narrator admits every piece of evidence against them; the repeated ‘Yes’ builds a list of facts that all point to their guilt, and ‘did happen to be’ sounds evasive.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: the evidence points to guilt / narrator is unreliable; reference to the repeated ‘Yes’ or the evasive ‘did happen to be’

items.stem: Read this sentence from the opening of a story, ‘Nobody Believes Me’: ‘which I have, for nearly a whole term’ What does this reveal about the narrator? Use point, evidence and explanation in your answer.
items.answer: The narrator is over-confident and exaggerates their expertise; ‘nearly a whole term’ is a tiny amount of study, which makes their claim comic.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: point (inference) + evidence (short quotation) + explanation of how the words create that impression. 1 mark: over-confident/boastful/naive; 1 mark: explains the humour of ‘nearly a whole term’.

items.stem: Read the opening of a story, ‘The Last Ferry’. ‘The last ferry of the season left without Mira. She reached the jetty in time to see its lights shrink across the black water, and for a long moment she simply stood there, her suitcase leaning against her leg like a tired dog. The ticket office was shuttered. A single gull picked at a crust beside the bins, unbothered. Behind her, the town climbed the hill in crooked steps, every window dark except one, high up near the church, where a lamp burned yellow and steady. Mira checked her phone again. No signal, just as there had been none since the bus crossed the bridge. Her aunt had promised to meet her. Her aunt had promised a great many things. She picked up the suitcase, turned towards the single light, and began to climb.’ What impressions of Mira does the writer create, and how?
items.answer: Lonely and let down (simile of the tired dog, repetition of ‘promised’), but determined (final sequence of verbs ‘picked up… turned… began to climb’).
items.markingKey: Level-marked: top band (4–5) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (2–3) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1) mainly retelling. [5]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is true of an unreliable narrator’s account? (b) What is an omniscient narrator?
items.answer: (a) cannot be fully trusted by the reader (b) A narrator who knows the thoughts and feelings of all the characters
items.markingKey: (a) Unreliable narrators may be biased, mistaken, lying or naive; the reader spots gaps between what is said and what happened. (b) Omniscient = all-knowing; often third person.

items.stem: Read this narrator’s account: ‘My brother always starts our fights. Today, for example, he started it by sitting in my chair, so I had no choice but to pour juice on his homework.’ Explain why the reader might not trust this narrator.
items.answer: The narrator blames the brother for a minor action while describing an extreme reaction of their own; ‘I had no choice’ is clearly untrue.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the gap between what the narrator claims and what the evidence shows; quotes the revealing detail; credit for explaining the effect (humour, sympathy or suspicion).

items.stem: Rewrite this extract using a different narrative viewpoint, then explain one thing that changes for the reader: ‘Kofi pressed his ear to the door. He could not make out the words, but he knew the argument was about him.’
items.answer: Model rewrite: ‘I pressed my ear to the door. I could not make out the words, but I knew the argument was about me.’ The change of viewpoint alters how close the reader is to the character’s thoughts.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for consistent change of pronouns and verb forms; 1 for keeping the meaning; remaining mark(s) for explaining the effect (closeness, knowledge, reliability). Original: third-person limited narrator.

items.stem: Write a story about a lost dog finding its way home, narrated by the dog. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Plan: the chase that leads the dog away; strange streets; a kind stranger misunderstood; the familiar smell of home; reunion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): an engaging, well-developed story with a clear, controlled structure; convincing characters and setting; tension or interest sustained; an effective ending; middle band (3–4): a clear story with some development of character and setting; structure mostly secure but pace may be uneven; lower band (1–2): a simple sequence of events with little development; structure unclear or ending abrupt. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: First-person animal narrator with a limited, distinctive view of human behaviour; humour or pathos from what the dog misunderstands; clear journey structure.

items.stem: Write an account of a busy market morning using a third-person omniscient narrator who reveals the thoughts of at least three different characters. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Plan: wide opening view of the market; stallholder worried about rent; shopper hiding a secret; child who has lost a coin; narrator links them in a final moment.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): an engaging, well-developed story with a clear, controlled structure; convincing characters and setting; tension or interest sustained; an effective ending; middle band (3–4): a clear story with some development of character and setting; structure mostly secure but pace may be uneven; lower band (1–2): a simple sequence of events with little development; structure unclear or ending abrupt. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: Moves between characters (a stallholder, a shopper, a child); reveals secret thoughts the others do not know; narrator may comment on events or hint at the future.

items.stem: Explain the effect of the words ‘as quick and careful as a bird building a nest’ in this line from an extract from a story, ‘The Radio Mender’: ‘mending radios with fingers as quick and careful as a bird building a nest’
items.answer: his hands are skilful, delicate and patient; the natural image suggests his work is instinctive and gentle.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘as quick and careful as a bird building a nest’. Model point: his hands are skilful, delicate and patient; the natural image suggests his work is instinctive and gentle. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Read: ‘looked at the coins, then at the boy’s worn shoes, and pushed the money back across the counter’ What does this suggest about the character? Explain how the writer shows this through what the character does (action).
items.answer: What the character does (action): his actions show he is observant and generous.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for identifying what the character does (action); further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: his actions show he is observant and generous.

items.stem: Identify the technique used in ‘“A thing done fast is a thing done twice,”’ (an extract from a story, ‘The Radio Mender’) and analyse its effect on the reader.
items.answer: Repetition (‘a thing done’): the balanced, repeated structure sounds like a proverb, showing his wisdom and his belief in doing work properly.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (repetition); 1 for selecting the key words ‘a thing done’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the balanced, repeated structure sounds like a proverb, showing his wisdom and his belief in doing work properly.

items.stem: This story opening is an example of opening with a description of the setting: ‘The desert at noon was white and silent, a sheet of glare stretching to the edge of the world.’ Explain the effect of opening in this way.
items.answer: Opening with a description of the setting: the harsh, empty setting suggests isolation and danger.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying opening with a description of the setting; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the harsh, empty setting suggests isolation and danger.

items.stem: Improve this opening so that it shows rather than tells: ‘Suddenly there was a loud noise and everyone was scared.’
items.answer: Model: ‘The crash came from the attic, a sound like a wardrobe falling down a staircase, and the dog crawled under the table.’ Specific sound and reactions replace vague words.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for: starting at an interesting moment; specific, vivid detail; a hook or question; accurate expression. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.
